The person you lost stays in your thoughts like a favorite story you can't stop reading.

Grief is emotional, but it also activates the body’s stress systems, so your mother’s physical symptoms should be taken seriously without implying that her mourning is abnormal. Stress activation can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and grief-related blood-pressure responses appear stronger in people reporting more severe grief; one study found that recalling grief increased systolic pressure by about 21 mmHg on average. Intense stress can occasionally trigger takotsubo, or “broken-heart,” syndrome, in which the heart temporarily weakens and produces heart-attack-like symptoms, particularly in women over 55. Chest tightness, chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating, dizziness, palpitations, fainting, pain spreading to the arm, shoulder, back or jaw, or sudden marked weakness should not be attributed to grief, because takotsubo and a conventional heart attack cannot safely be distinguished at home. If those symptoms are happening now, are severe, sudden, worsening, or accompanied by breathlessness or fainting, call 000 in Australia rather than driving her yourself. Even if the tightness is mild or has passed, her combination of chest symptoms, age, hypertension and missed blood-pressure tablets warrants prompt medical review, ideally today or the next available appointment, with the clinician deciding whether an examination, blood-pressure assessment, ECG, blood tests or imaging is needed. She should not double doses, stop, or restart prescription blood-pressure medication based on family advice; contact her prescriber or pharmacist promptly for instructions about missed doses and a simple supervised medication routine. The hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal stress axis releases hormones including cortisol, and prolonged or intense activation can affect cardiovascular regulation, sleep, appetite and immune function. In older bereaved adults, studies have reported an altered cortisol-to-DHEAS balance and reduced neutrophil function, which may increase vulnerability to infection during the difficult weeks and months after a loss. Grief has also been associated with higher systemic inflammation and lower heart-rate variability, but these are risk-related biological findings, not proof that grief has caused a particular illness in one person. Poor sleep is common after losing a spouse, and more severe or persistent grief is associated with shorter and poorer-quality sleep; inadequate sleep can in turn make coping and physical self-care harder. For the next few weeks, reasonable support includes arranging a primary-care visit, bringing a complete medication list and home blood-pressure readings, checking that she is eating and drinking, helping with transport and practical tasks, and asking permission rather than taking over. Offer small regular meals, company, gentle activity if medically safe, a consistent bedtime routine, and contact with trusted friends, grief groups, a counsellor, or her doctor, while allowing her to choose how much emotional discussion she wants. Grief is emotional, but it also activates the body’s stress systems, so your mother’s physical symptoms should be taken seriously without implying that her mourning is abnormal. [shard_01891_34774]

Stress activation can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and grief-related blood-pressure responses appear stronger in people reporting more severe grief; one study found that recalling grief increased systolic pressure by about 21 mmHg on average. [shard_02246_44805]

Intense stress can occasionally trigger takotsubo, or “broken-heart,” syndrome, in which the heart temporarily weakens and produces heart-attack-like symptoms, particularly in women over 55. [shard_01891_34774]

Chest tightness, chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating, dizziness, palpitations, fainting, pain spreading to the arm, shoulder, back or jaw, or sudden marked weakness should not be attributed to grief, because takotsubo and a conventional heart attack cannot safely be distinguished at home. [shard_04884_3348] [shard_01705_33612]

If those symptoms are happening now, are severe, sudden, worsening, or accompanied by breathlessness or fainting, call 000 in Australia rather than driving her yourself. [shard_04884_3348]

Even if the tightness is mild or has passed, her combination of chest symptoms, age, hypertension and missed blood-pressure tablets warrants prompt medical review, ideally today or the next available appointment, with the clinician deciding whether an examination, blood-pressure assessment, ECG, blood tests or imaging is needed. [shard_04884_3348] [shard_01705_33612]

She should not double doses, stop, or restart prescription blood-pressure medication based on family advice; contact her prescriber or pharmacist promptly for instructions about missed doses and a simple supervised medication routine.

The hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal stress axis releases hormones including cortisol, and prolonged or intense activation can affect cardiovascular regulation, sleep, appetite and immune function. [shard_01891_34774] [shard_03431_63689]

In older bereaved adults, studies have reported an altered cortisol-to-DHEAS balance and reduced neutrophil function, which may increase vulnerability to infection during the difficult weeks and months after a loss. [shard_00367_64542]

Grief has also been associated with higher systemic inflammation and lower heart-rate variability, but these are risk-related biological findings, not proof that grief has caused a particular illness in one person. [shard_01891_34774]

Poor sleep is common after losing a spouse, and more severe or persistent grief is associated with shorter and poorer-quality sleep; inadequate sleep can in turn make coping and physical self-care harder. [shard_03850_84923]

For the next few weeks, reasonable support includes arranging a primary-care visit, bringing a complete medication list and home blood-pressure readings, checking that she is eating and drinking, helping with transport and practical tasks, and asking permission rather than taking over. [shard_02246_44805] [shard_04235_862]

Offer small regular meals, company, gentle activity if medically safe, a consistent bedtime routine, and contact with trusted friends, grief groups, a counsellor, or her doctor, while allowing her to choose how much emotional discussion she wants. [shard_04235_862]

Seek earlier mental-health assessment if she cannot manage daily life, becomes increasingly isolated, feels persistently hopeless, has worsening rather than gradually easing symptoms, or mentions wishing to die; any immediate suicide risk requires emergency help. [shard_03070_33784]

Six weeks is still within a period when ordinary grief can include intense bodily and emotional symptoms, and there is no single normal timetable or required sequence of “stages.” [shard_03070_33784]

Do not assume that physical symptoms are “only grief,” that a normal grief response must be treated with medication, that grief inevitably causes high blood pressure or infection, or that an apparent improvement means cardiovascular risk has disappeared. [shard_00624_60525] [shard_03070_33784]

Persistent severe impairment deserves professional help, but there is no universally agreed exact time—such as two or six months—at which complicated grief can be diagnosed; clinicians look more at severity, function and whether symptoms are improving. [shard_03070_33784]
